skills.graph: The right curve on the right graph, labeled, shifted the right way, with the new equilibrium compared with the old
skills.marginal: The marginal rule stated with the numbers: MR = MC for output, MRP = MRC for hiring, MB = MC or MU per dollar for a consumer
skills.price: Price read from the demand curve above the quantity where MR = MC, never from MR or MC
skills.area: The right region named and bounded: consumer or producer surplus, tax revenue, subsidy cost, profit, deadweight loss
skills.compare: A game theory claim with both comparisons from the matrix (dominant strategy, best response, Nash equilibrium)
skills.longrun: The long-run chain with every link: profit or loss, entry or exit, market supply shifts, price returns to minimum ATC
skills.derived: The derived-demand chain with every link: product demand, product price (MR), MRP, labor demand, wage and hiring
skills.efficiency: Market quantity compared with the efficient quantity (MSB = MSC), with the deadweight loss and the corrective policy
skills.calculate: A calculation with the formula or steps shown, not the answer alone
skills.identify: An explicit statement of the concept, quantity or outcome asked for

prompts.title: The opportunity cost, not money already spent
prompts.prompt: Identify the opportunity cost of a student's Saturday spent at a paid internship, when she has already paid a $40 nonrefundable concert ticket for that day and her next-best choice is a $90 shift at a cafe.
checklist: Names the next-best alternative given up: the $90 cafe shift
Says the $40 ticket is a sunk cost, paid whatever she does
Does not add the ticket to the opportunity cost

earns.answer: The opportunity cost of the internship day is the $90 cafe shift, her next-best alternative. The $40 concert ticket is a sunk cost: it is paid and cannot be refunded whatever she chooses, so it is not part of the opportunity cost.
earns.why: It names the single next-best alternative and keeps the sunk cost out.

misses.answer: Her opportunity cost is $130: the ticket plus the cafe shift.
misses.why: The ticket is spent either way; adding it counts a sunk cost as part of the choice.

why.1: The ticket is paid whatever she does, so it is not given up by this choice.
why.2: The ticket is a sunk cost; the cost of the choice is the next-best alternative.

why.1: It cannot be recovered whichever choice she makes, so it is sunk.

prompts.title: Who decides what gets made
prompts.prompt: Explain how a market economy and a command economy each decide how many bicycles to make.
checklist: Says that in a market economy prices lead firms to make what buyers will pay for
Says that in a command economy a central plan sets the quantity
Names the decision maker in each

earns.answer: In a market economy, firms make more bicycles when buyers will pay a price that covers their costs and more, so prices steer how many are made. In a command economy, a central planning authority sets the number of bicycles in its plan, whatever buyers would pay.
earns.why: It names the decision maker and the signal in each system.

misses.answer: In a market economy people decide, and in a command economy the government decides.
misses.why: It does not say how the decision is made: the price signal and the plan are both missing.

market.label: In a market economy the quantity follows

why.1: A plan is the command method; markets use prices.

command.label: In a command economy the quantity is set by

why.1: Willingness to pay steers a market economy, not a planned one.

prompts.title: Opportunity cost per unit from a PPC
prompts.prompt: Calculate the opportunity cost of one more chair when a workshop moves along its PPC from 20 chairs and 60 tables to 30 chairs and 40 tables.
checklist: Finds the tables given up: 60 - 40
Divides by the chairs gained: 30 - 20
States the answer in tables per chair

earns.answer: Moving along the PPC, the workshop gives up 60 - 40 = 20 tables to gain 30 - 20 = 10 chairs. The opportunity cost of one more chair is 20 / 10 = 2 tables per chair.
earns.why: It shows what is given up and what is gained, divides, and gives the unit.

misses.answer: The opportunity cost of one more chair is 20 tables, the tables given up.
misses.why: That is the cost of all 10 chairs together, not of one chair, and the unit per chair is missing.

why.1: 40 is how many tables are left, not how many are given up.
why.2: 10 is the number of chairs gained.

why.1: That is for 10 chairs; divide by 10.
why.2: That is chairs per table: the ratio is upside down.

prompts.title: Why a PPC bows out
prompts.prompt: Explain why a farm's PPC for corn and beans is bowed out from the origin.
checklist: Says resources are not equally suited to both goods
Says each extra unit of corn costs more beans than the last: increasing opportunity cost
Links the rising opportunity cost to the bowed-out shape

earns.answer: Some fields suit corn and others suit beans. As the farm grows more corn, it has to switch fields that are better for beans, so each extra unit of corn costs more beans than the one before. That increasing opportunity cost makes the PPC bowed out from the origin.
earns.why: It gives the reason (resources suited to one good) and links increasing opportunity cost to the shape.

misses.answer: The PPC is bowed out because the farm cannot make more of both goods.
misses.why: That explains why the PPC slopes down, a tradeoff, not why it bows out.

cost.label: As corn rises, each extra unit costs

why.1: A constant cost gives a straight-line PPC.
why.2: Falling cost gives a PPC bowed in.

why.label: The reason is that resources are
options: not equally suited to both goods

why.1: Resources are moved between goods, not used up; their fit differs.

prompts.title: Investing in capital moves the PPC
prompts.prompt: Draw and explain what happens to a country's PPC for consumer goods and capital goods in later years if it makes more capital goods now.
checklist: Shows the PPC shifting outward in later years
Says the reason: more capital raises what the country can produce
Labels the new curve PPC2 outside PPC1

earns.answer: Making more capital goods now gives the country more machines and tools later, which raises how much it can produce. So in later years its PPC shifts outward from PPC1 to PPC2, and it can make more of both goods.
earns.why: It gives the shift, its direction and the reason, with the new curve labeled.

misses.answer: The country moves along its PPC toward capital goods.
misses.why: That is the choice this year; the question asks about later years, when the curve itself shifts out.

why.1: More capital adds to what the country can make; it does not shrink.
why.2: The added capital changes what can be produced, so the curve moves.

why.1: Wants do not move the PPC; a change in resources does.

prompts.title: Comparative advantage from opportunity costs
prompts.prompt: Determine which workshop has the comparative advantage in tables. In a day, Ardent can make 10 chairs or 5 tables, and Birch can make 9 chairs or 3 tables. Show your work.
checklist: Finds each workshop's opportunity cost of a table in chairs
Compares the two opportunity costs of a table
Gives the comparative advantage to the lower opportunity cost

earns.answer: A table costs Ardent 10 / 5 = 2 chairs and costs Birch 9 / 3 = 3 chairs. Ardent gives up fewer chairs per table, so Ardent has the comparative advantage in tables.
earns.why: Both opportunity costs are calculated and compared, and the lower one wins.

misses.answer: Ardent has the comparative advantage in tables because it makes more tables, 5 against 3.
misses.why: Making more is absolute advantage; comparative advantage needs the opportunity costs.

why.1: That is tables per chair; the ratio is upside down.
why.2: That is its output, not what a table costs it.

who.label: Comparative advantage in tables goes to

why.1: Birch gives up 3 chairs per table, more than Ardent's 2.
why.2: The costs differ, so one workshop has the advantage.

prompts.title: A price for trade that helps both
prompts.prompt: Identify a price of one table, in chairs, at which both Ardent (a table costs it 2 chairs) and Birch (a table costs it 3 chairs) gain from trade, and explain why.
checklist: Gives a price strictly between the two opportunity costs
Says Ardent sells tables for more than they cost it
Says Birch buys tables for less than making them

earns.answer: A price of 2.5 chairs per table helps both. Ardent sells each table for 2.5 chairs though it costs Ardent 2, and Birch gets a table for 2.5 chairs though making one costs Birch 3. Any price between 2 and 3 chairs works.
earns.why: It gives a price between the two costs and shows each side gains.

misses.answer: They should trade one table for one chair, so the trade is fair.
misses.why: At 1 chair Ardent gets less than its own cost of 2 chairs, so it loses.

why.1: Below Ardent's cost of 2 chairs, Ardent loses.
why.2: Above Birch's cost of 3 chairs, Birch would make its own.

why.1: Above both, the buyer gains nothing from trading.

prompts.title: Net benefit with an implicit cost
prompts.prompt: Calculate the net benefit of Maya's summer bike-repair stand. It takes in $7,000, she pays $2,500 for parts and space, and she gives up a summer job paying $3,000. Show your work.
checklist: Subtracts the money paid out (explicit cost)
Subtracts the job she gives up (implicit cost)
States whether the stand is the better choice

earns.answer: Net benefit counts both kinds of cost: 7,000 - 2,500 - 3,000 = $1,500. The stand earns $1,500 more than the job she gives up, so it is the better choice.
earns.why: Both costs come off, with the numbers shown and the decision stated.

misses.answer: Her net benefit is 7,000 - 2,500 = $4,500, so the stand is a good idea.
misses.why: It leaves out the $3,000 job she gives up, an implicit cost.

why.1: The job she gives up is a cost of the choice too.
That leaves out the implicit cost.
why.2: Costs are subtracted, not added.

prompts.title: When to stop: marginal benefit and marginal cost
prompts.prompt: Explain how many hours a student should tutor if the third hour brings a marginal benefit of $15 at a marginal cost of $12, and the fourth brings $10 at $14.
checklist: Compares marginal benefit with marginal cost hour by hour
Keeps going while MB is at least MC and stops before MB falls below MC
Gives the number of hours: 3

earns.answer: Do each hour while its marginal benefit is at least its marginal cost, stopping near MB = MC. The third hour adds $15 of benefit for $12 of cost, so it is worth doing. The fourth adds $10 for $14, so it is not. The student should tutor 3 hours.
earns.why: It states the marginal rule and applies it to both hours with the numbers.

misses.answer: She should tutor 4 hours, because the total benefit is still positive.
misses.why: Total benefit is not the test: the fourth hour costs more than it adds.

rule.label: Do another hour while
options: its MB is at least its MC

why.1: Total benefit can be positive while the last hour loses value.
The fourth hour's MB ($10) is below its MC ($14).
why.2: The third hour adds more than it costs, so stopping at 2 leaves value.

prompts.title: Marginal utility per dollar
prompts.prompt: Explain whether Jonah should spend his next $20 on two books ($10 each, the next book gives 40 utils) or one concert ticket ($20, giving 60 utils), using marginal utility per dollar.
checklist: Divides each marginal utility by its price
Compares the two utils-per-dollar ratios
Chooses the good with the higher MU per dollar

earns.answer: Compare marginal utility per dollar, MU / P. The next book gives 40 / 10 = 4 utils per dollar and the ticket 60 / 20 = 3 utils per dollar. A book gives more per dollar, so Jonah should spend on books first.
earns.why: It divides by price, compares the ratios and decides.

misses.answer: Jonah should buy the concert ticket because 60 utils is more than 40.
misses.why: It compares marginal utility without dividing by price, which is the slip readers report.

why.1: A more expensive good must give more utility to be worth it; divide by price.
That compares totals, not utility per dollar.

prompts.title: Own price or income: move or shift
prompts.prompt: Explain the difference on a demand graph for pizza between a fall in the price of pizza and a rise in buyers' incomes, if pizza is a normal good.
checklist: Says a fall in pizza's own price is a movement down along D to a larger quantity demanded
Says a rise in income shifts demand for a normal good to the right
Labels the new demand curve D2, to the right

earns.answer: A fall in the price of pizza is a movement down along the demand curve: quantity demanded rises, but demand does not change. A rise in incomes, for a normal good, increases demand: the whole curve shifts right from D1 to D2, so more is demanded at every price.
earns.why: It keeps the two apart, a change in quantity demanded and a change in demand, with the direction and the new curve.

misses.answer: Both make people buy more pizza, so both shift demand to the right.
misses.why: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only the income change shifts it.

why.1: Price is on the axis, so its change is a movement along the curve.
For a normal good, more income means more demand, not less.
why.2: Income is not on an axis, so the curve shifts.

prompts.title: Price elasticity and the total revenue test
prompts.prompt: Calculate the price elasticity of demand when a cafe raises the price of a smoothie from $4 to $5 and sales fall from 200 to 140 a day (use percent changes from the original values), and say what happens to total revenue.
checklist: Shows the percent change in quantity and in price
Divides quantity over price and reads the absolute value
Uses the total revenue test: elastic, so revenue falls when the price rises

earns.answer: Quantity changes by (140 - 200) / 200 x 100 = -30% and price by (5 - 4) / 4 x 100 = 25%. The elasticity is 30% / 25% = 1.2, above 1, so demand is elastic. Revenue falls from $800 to $700, as the total revenue test says for an elastic range.
earns.why: Both percent changes are shown, quantity goes on top, and the revenue test follows from the elasticity.

misses.answer: The elasticity is 60 / 1 = 60, so demand is very elastic.
misses.why: That divides the changes in units, not percent changes, so it is a slope, not an elasticity.

why.1: The ratio is quantity over price; upside down it gives 0.83.
With elastic demand a price rise loses more in sales than it gains per unit.
why.2: Revenue is unchanged only with unit elastic demand.

prompts.title: The total revenue test in words
prompts.prompt: Explain why a bus company with inelastic demand for rides raises its total revenue when it raises fares.
checklist: Says inelastic means quantity falls by a smaller percent than the price rises
Says the gain per ride outweighs the rides lost
Concludes that total revenue (price x quantity) rises

earns.answer: With inelastic demand, a fare rise lowers the number of rides by a smaller percent than the fare rises. The company gains more on each ride it still sells than it loses on the rides it no longer sells, so total revenue, fare times rides, rises.
earns.why: It defines inelastic in percent changes and links it to revenue.

misses.answer: Revenue rises because the fares are higher.
misses.why: Higher fares alone do not decide it: the answer has to compare the price change with the fall in rides.

def.label: Inelastic means rides fall
options: by a smaller percent than the fare rises
by a larger percent than the fare rises

why.1: That is elastic demand.
The gain per ride outweighs the rides lost when demand is inelastic.

prompts.title: Cross-price elasticity and its sign
prompts.prompt: Calculate the cross-price elasticity of demand for jelly when the price of peanut butter rises from $5 to $6 and jelly sales fall from 100 to 90 jars, and say how the goods are related.
checklist: Shows the percent change in jelly sales and in the peanut butter price
Keeps the sign of the result
Says a negative value means complements

earns.answer: Jelly sales change by (90 - 100) / 100 x 100 = -10% and the price of peanut butter by (6 - 5) / 5 x 100 = 20%. The cross-price elasticity is -10% / 20% = -0.5. It is negative, so jelly and peanut butter are complements.
earns.why: It shows both changes, keeps the sign and reads the relationship from it.

misses.answer: The cross-price elasticity is 0.5, so the goods are substitutes.
misses.why: Dropping the sign loses the answer: the value is negative, so the goods are complements.

why.1: The sign is the answer here; jelly sales fell, so it is negative.
why.2: That divides the price change by the quantity change.

why.1: Substitutes have a positive cross-price elasticity.
why.2: Jelly sales responded, so they are related.

prompts.title: Consumer surplus as a triangle
prompts.prompt: Calculate consumer surplus in a market where the equilibrium price is $6, 40 units are sold, and the demand curve is a straight line that reaches the price axis at $10, and say which area it is.
checklist: Names the area: below demand and above the price, out to the quantity bought
Uses one half times base times height
Shows the numbers with the price gap $10 - $6

earns.answer: Consumer surplus is the triangle below the demand curve and above the $6 price, out to 40 units: 1/2 x 40 x ($10 - $6) = $80.
earns.why: It names the region and shows the triangle formula with the right height.

misses.answer: Consumer surplus is what buyers spend: 40 x $6 = $240.
misses.why: That is what buyers pay (total revenue), not the surplus above the price.

why.1: That is producer surplus.
That leaves out the one half.
why.2: That is total spending, price times quantity.

prompts.title: A cost increase on the supply and demand graph
prompts.prompt: Draw a correctly labeled graph of the market for bread and show the effect of a rise in the price of flour on the equilibrium price and quantity.
checklist: Shifts supply to the left (S1 to S2), leaving demand in place
Shows the new equilibrium at a higher price and a lower quantity
Labels the axes, both supply curves and P1, P2, Q1, Q2

earns.answer: Flour is an input, so its higher price raises the cost of making bread and supply shifts left from S1 to S2. Demand does not move. At the new equilibrium the price rises from P1 to P2 and the quantity falls from Q1 to Q2, all labeled on the axes.
earns.why: The right curve shifts the right way and both outcomes are compared with the old equilibrium.

misses.answer: Bread costs more, so demand shifts left and the price falls.
misses.why: An input price moves supply, not demand, and the price of bread rises.

why.1: Buyers' wants did not change; the cost of making bread did.
why.2: Higher costs shift supply left, not right.

why.1: A leftward supply shift raises the price along demand.

prompts.title: Two shifts at once: what can be known
prompts.prompt: Explain what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity of coffee when demand increases and supply decreases at the same time.
checklist: Says the price rises, since both shifts push it up
Says the change in quantity is indeterminate
Gives the reason: the shifts push quantity in opposite directions and their sizes are not known

earns.answer: Both changes raise the price: more demand pushes it up and less supply pushes it up, so the price rises. The quantity is indeterminate, because the demand increase raises it and the supply decrease lowers it, and without the sizes of the shifts we cannot tell which wins.
earns.why: It states the known change, calls the other indeterminate and says why.

misses.answer: The price rises and the quantity stays the same.
misses.why: Quantity is not known to stay the same; it could rise or fall, so "indeterminate" is the answer.

why.1: Both shifts push the price up.
why.2: Both push the same way, so the price change is known.

why.1: The supply decrease could outweigh the demand increase.
why.2: Nothing pins the quantity; it depends on the sizes of the shifts.

prompts.title: Tax revenue and deadweight loss
prompts.prompt: Calculate the government's revenue and the deadweight loss of a $2 per-unit tax that lowers the quantity sold from 50 to 40 units, and say which areas they are.
checklist: Tax revenue: tax per unit times the quantity after the tax
Deadweight loss: the triangle between demand and supply over the units no longer sold
Shows both with numbers, including the one half

earns.answer: Tax revenue is the rectangle between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep, out to the new quantity: $2 x 40 = $80. The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and supply over the 10 units no longer sold: 1/2 x 10 x $2 = $10.
earns.why: Each area is named and bounded, with the quantity after the tax and the one half.

misses.answer: Tax revenue is $2 x 50 = $100, and there is no loss because the government gets the money.
misses.why: Revenue uses the quantity after the tax, and the lost trades are a deadweight loss nobody gets.

why.1: The tax is collected on the 40 units still sold, not the old 50.

dwl.label: Deadweight loss
options: \$10, the triangle on the 10 lost units

why.1: A triangle needs the one half.
why.2: The 10 units no longer traded are a real loss.

prompts.title: The shortage at a binding ceiling
prompts.prompt: Calculate the shortage when a city caps rent at $800 a month, below equilibrium, and at $800 renters want 900 apartments while landlords offer 600.
checklist: Says the ceiling binds because it is below equilibrium
Subtracts quantity supplied from quantity demanded at the ceiling
Says the quantity rented is the smaller one, 600

earns.answer: The ceiling is below equilibrium, so it binds. At $800, quantity demanded is 900 and quantity supplied is 600, a shortage of 900 - 600 = 300 apartments. Only 600 are rented, the quantity landlords supply.
earns.why: It compares the two quantities at the ceiling and says how many are actually rented.

misses.answer: There is a shortage because the price is too low for landlords.
misses.why: It names the shortage but never sizes it, and the question asks for the number.

why.1: A shortage is the gap between the two quantities, not their sum.
why.2: 600 is the quantity supplied, the number rented.

why.1: Renters cannot rent units landlords do not offer.

prompts.title: Imports and revenue with a tariff
prompts.prompt: Calculate imports and tariff revenue when a $1 tariff raises the price of rice from the $3 world price to $4, and at $4 buyers want 50 tons while domestic farms supply 30, and name the area.
checklist: Imports: quantity demanded minus quantity supplied at the price with the tariff
Tariff revenue: the tariff times imports after the tariff
Names the rectangle: between the two prices, over the imports

earns.answer: At $4, imports are quantity demanded minus domestic quantity supplied: 50 - 30 = 20 tons. Tariff revenue is the rectangle between $3 and $4 over those imports: $1 x 20 = $20.
earns.why: It finds imports after the tariff and names and sizes the revenue rectangle.

misses.answer: Tariff revenue is the tariff on all the rice: $1 x 50 = $50.
misses.why: The tariff is paid on imports only, not on rice from domestic farms.

why.1: That is all rice bought; domestic farms supply 30 of it.
why.2: That is domestic supply.

why.1: Domestic rice pays no tariff.
why.2: That multiplies by the price, not by the tariff.

prompts.title: Where diminishing marginal returns begin
prompts.prompt: Identify the worker with whom diminishing marginal returns begin, for a shop with one oven whose output is 10, 24, 34 and 40 pizzas with 1, 2, 3 and 4 workers. Show your work.
checklist: Finds marginal product as the change in output from each added worker
Finds where marginal product starts to fall
Names the fixed input as the reason

earns.answer: Marginal product is the change in output: 10, then 24 - 10 = 14, then 34 - 24 = 10, then 6. It rises with the second worker and falls with the third, so diminishing marginal returns begin with the third worker: the workers share one fixed oven.
earns.why: It computes each marginal product and names where it starts falling and why.

misses.answer: Diminishing returns begin with the fourth worker, because 40 is the most output.
misses.why: Total output still rises; the test is marginal product, which falls from the third worker on.

why.1: That is total output with three workers.
why.2: That is average product, 34 / 3.

why.1: MP already fell with the third worker.
why.2: The second worker's MP (14) is higher than the first's.

prompts.title: Marginal cost when output changes by more than 1
prompts.prompt: Calculate the marginal cost per unit when a firm's output rises from 50 to 70 units and its total cost rises from $400 to $520.
checklist: Uses MC = change in total cost / change in output
Divides by the change in output, 20, not by 1
States the answer per unit

earns.answer: Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output: ($520 - $400) / (70 - 50) = $6 per unit.
earns.why: It shows the formula with both changes and divides by the change in output.

misses.answer: The marginal cost is $520 - $400 = $120.
misses.why: That is the change in total cost for 20 units together; per unit, divide by 20.

div.label: Divide the change in total cost by

why.1: Output rose by 20 units, not 1.
why.2: Dividing by output gives an average, not a marginal cost.

why.1: That is the change for all 20 units.
why.2: That is ATC at 70 units.

prompts.title: MC crosses AVC and ATC at their lowest points
prompts.prompt: Explain why the marginal cost curve crosses the average total cost curve at its lowest point.
checklist: Says that when MC is below ATC, the next unit pulls the average down
Says that when MC is above ATC, it pulls the average up
Concludes that ATC is lowest where MC equals it, so MC crosses at the minimum

earns.answer: When the cost of one more unit (MC) is below the average (ATC), producing it pulls the average down, so ATC falls. When MC is above ATC, it pulls the average up, so ATC rises. ATC stops falling and starts rising exactly where MC equals it, so MC crosses ATC at its lowest point, and the same logic holds for AVC.
earns.why: It gives the marginal-average rule both ways and draws the conclusion for the crossing.

misses.answer: MC crosses ATC at the bottom because that is how the graph is drawn.
misses.why: It gives no reason; the marginal-average rule is the explanation.

below.label: When MC is below ATC, ATC

why.1: A unit cheaper than the average pulls the average down.
While ATC falls, MC is still below it.
why.2: The shutdown point is the lowest point of AVC, not ATC.

prompts.title: A fixed cost moves ATC, not MC
prompts.prompt: Explain how a rise in a firm's yearly license fee, a fixed cost, changes its MC, AVC and ATC curves and its profit-maximizing output.
checklist: Says ATC (and AFC) shift up
Says MC and AVC do not change
Says output where MR = MC stays the same

earns.answer: A license fee is fixed: it does not change with output. It raises AFC, so ATC shifts up. MC and AVC depend only on variable costs, so they do not move. Because MC is unchanged, the output where MR = MC is unchanged; only profit falls.
earns.why: It separates the curves that move from those that do not and follows through to output.

misses.answer: All the cost curves shift up, so the firm produces less.
misses.why: A fixed cost leaves MC in place, so the profit-maximizing output does not change.

why.1: A fixed cost is not part of variable cost or marginal cost.
why.2: MC depends on variable costs only.

why.1: MC did not move, so MR still meets it at the same quantity.

prompts.title: Accounting profit and economic profit
prompts.prompt: Calculate the accounting profit and the economic profit of a bakery with $200,000 in revenue, $150,000 in explicit costs and an owner who gives up a $60,000 salary.
checklist: Accounting profit: revenue minus explicit costs
Economic profit: also subtracts the implicit cost
Says the result is an economic loss

earns.answer: Accounting profit is 200,000 - 150,000 = $50,000. Economic profit also subtracts the $60,000 salary the owner gives up, an implicit cost: 50,000 - 60,000 = -$10,000, an economic loss.
earns.why: Both profits are calculated, the implicit cost is named and the loss is stated.

misses.answer: The bakery makes a profit of $50,000, so it is doing well.
misses.why: That is accounting profit only; with the forgone salary the owner earns less than her best alternative.

why.1: That is economic profit.
why.2: That is revenue, before any cost.

why.1: The salary is a cost: subtract it.
why.2: That leaves out the implicit cost.

prompts.title: Choose output with MR = MC
prompts.prompt: Explain how many units a perfectly competitive firm should make at a price of $12 if the marginal cost of the 5th, 6th and 7th units is $10, $11 and $13.
checklist: States the rule: produce where MR = MC (MR equals the price here)
Compares MR with MC for each unit
Gives the output: 6 units

earns.answer: A competitive firm's MR equals the price, $12. It produces each unit whose MR is at least its MC, up to MR = MC: the 5th ($12 against $10) and the 6th ($12 against $11) add to profit, the 7th ($12 against $13) does not. It makes 6 units.
earns.why: It states the marginal rule and checks each unit with the numbers.

misses.answer: It should make 7 units, because the price is close to the marginal cost.
misses.why: The 7th unit costs $13 and brings in $12, so it lowers profit.

why.1: That is the break-even point, not the profit-maximizing rule.
why.2: Units with MC above MR lower profit.

why.1: The 7th unit's MC is above MR.
why.2: The 6th unit still adds $1 to profit.

prompts.title: The shutdown rule with numbers
prompts.prompt: Explain whether a competitive firm should shut down in the short run at a price of $5, if at its best output of 100 units its ATC is $8 and its AVC is $6.
checklist: Compares the price with AVC, not ATC
Calculates the loss from producing and from shutting down
Concludes: shut down, since the price is below AVC

earns.answer: Producing loses ($5 - $8) x 100 = -$300. Shutting down loses only the fixed cost, ($8 - $6) x 100 = $200. The price is below AVC, so the firm cannot even cover its variable costs and should shut down, losing $200 instead of $300.
earns.why: It applies the price-AVC test and shows both losses.

misses.answer: It should keep producing because it has to pay its fixed costs anyway.
misses.why: Fixed costs are paid either way; producing adds a loss on every unit, since the price is below AVC.

why.1: Below ATC the firm makes a loss but may still produce; the shutdown test is AVC.
why.2: The test is price against average variable cost.

why.1: At $5 the price is below its $6 AVC.

prompts.title: The competitive firm's demand curve
prompts.prompt: Draw and explain the demand curve a perfectly competitive firm faces, next to the market graph that sets the price.
checklist: Shows the market price set where market supply meets market demand
Draws the firm's demand as a horizontal line at that price
Labels it d = MR = AR = P

earns.answer: The market price is set where market supply meets market demand, on the left graph. The firm is a price taker, so on the right graph its demand curve is a horizontal line at that price, labeled d = MR = AR = P: it can sell any amount at the market price, so each unit adds the price to revenue.
earns.why: It ties the firm's line to the market price and labels it fully.

misses.answer: The firm's demand slopes down like the market demand curve.
misses.why: A price taker can sell any amount at the market price, so its demand is horizontal.

why.1: That is the market's demand; one firm cannot move the price.
why.2: The firm can vary its quantity freely at the price.

why.1: MC is the firm's cost curve, not its demand.

prompts.title: From profit to the long run
prompts.prompt: Explain what happens in the long run in a perfectly competitive industry whose firms are earning economic profit.
checklist: Says profit attracts new firms (entry)
Says market supply shifts right, so the price falls
Says entry stops when the price reaches minimum ATC and economic profit is zero

earns.answer: Economic profit draws new firms into the industry. Entry shifts market supply to the right, which lowers the market price. Firms' profits fall, and entry continues until the price falls to the lowest point of ATC, where economic profit is zero.
earns.why: Every link is there: profit, entry, supply shifts, the price falls to minimum ATC.

misses.answer: In the long run the profit goes away and price equals ATC.
misses.why: It states the end point but skips entry and the supply shift that get there.

why.1: Exit follows losses, not profits.

shift.label: Market supply
options: shifts right, so the price falls
shifts left, so the price rises

why.1: More firms mean more supply at each price.
At minimum AVC firms still make a loss.

prompts.title: From losses to the long run
prompts.prompt: Explain what happens in the long run in a perfectly competitive industry whose firms are earning economic losses.
checklist: Says losses lead some firms to exit
Says market supply shifts left, so the price rises
Says exit stops when the price reaches minimum ATC

earns.answer: Losses lead some firms to exit the industry. Exit shifts market supply to the left, which raises the market price. Losses shrink, and exit continues until the price rises to the lowest point of ATC, where the remaining firms earn zero economic profit.
earns.why: It links losses, exit, the supply shift and the price back to minimum ATC.

misses.answer: Firms keep losing money until demand rises again.
misses.why: The long-run fix comes from exit shifting supply, not from waiting for demand.

why.1: Losses keep new firms out and push some out.

shift.label: Market supply
options: shifts left, so the price rises
shifts right, so the price falls

why.1: Fewer firms mean less supply at each price.

prompts.title: Why a monopoly's profit lasts
prompts.prompt: Explain why a monopoly can keep earning economic profit in the long run when a perfectly competitive firm cannot.
checklist: Names a barrier to entry (a patent, control of a key resource, economies of scale)
Says the barrier keeps rivals from entering
Contrasts it with free entry competing profit away in perfect competition

earns.answer: A monopoly is protected by a barrier to entry, such as a patent or control of a key resource, so new firms cannot come in and add supply. In perfect competition entry is free, so profit draws new firms until the price falls to minimum ATC; the barrier stops that from happening to the monopoly.
earns.why: It names a barrier and says what it blocks: entry.

misses.answer: A monopoly can charge whatever price it wants, so its profit lasts.
misses.why: It is still limited by demand, and the answer leaves out the barrier to entry, which is the reason.

why.1: A horizontal demand curve describes a price taker.
why.2: Low cost alone does not keep rivals out.

why.1: Demand can change; what is blocked is entry.

prompts.title: The monopoly price comes from demand
prompts.prompt: Explain how a profit-maximizing monopolist chooses its price, if MR = MC = $8 at 30 units and the demand curve shows a price of $14 at 30 units.
checklist: Finds the quantity where MR = MC: 30 units
Reads the price up on the demand curve at that quantity: $14
Does not set the price at MR or MC

earns.answer: The monopolist first finds the quantity where MR = MC, 30 units. It then charges the highest price buyers will pay for 30 units, read up on the demand curve: $14. The price is above the $8 marginal cost.
earns.why: It finds the quantity first and reads the price from demand.

misses.answer: The monopolist charges $8, where MR = MC.
misses.why: MR = MC picks the quantity; the price is read from demand above it.

why.1: That is the efficient quantity, not the monopoly's choice.
why.2: The monopoly does not produce at minimum ATC.

why.1: Buyers will pay $14 for 30 units, so the monopolist charges that.

prompts.title: The fair-return price for a natural monopoly
prompts.prompt: Explain where a regulator should set the price of a natural monopoly if it wants zero economic profit, and why setting the price at marginal cost would need a subsidy.
checklist: Sets the fair-return price where demand meets ATC
Says P = ATC gives zero economic profit
Says ATC lies above MC over the range of demand, so P = MC leaves a loss

earns.answer: The fair-return price is read from the demand curve where it crosses ATC: there price equals average total cost, so economic profit is zero. Because ATC falls over the whole range of demand, it lies above MC, so a price where demand meets MC would be below ATC and the firm would need a subsidy.
earns.why: It reads the price from demand at ATC and explains the loss at P = MC.

misses.answer: The regulator should set the price where MR = MC so the firm breaks even.
misses.why: MR = MC is the unregulated monopoly choice; zero profit is where demand meets ATC.

why.1: That is the unregulated monopoly output.
why.2: That is the socially optimal price, which leaves a loss.

loss.label: At P = MC the firm makes a loss because

why.1: For a natural monopoly ATC falls over the demand range and stays above MC.

prompts.title: The monopoly's deadweight loss
prompts.prompt: Identify the deadweight loss on a correctly labeled monopoly graph and explain why it exists.
checklist: Bounds the area: between demand and MC, from the monopoly quantity to where demand meets MC
Says the monopoly produces less than the efficient quantity
Says those units are worth more to buyers than they cost to make

earns.answer: The monopoly produces where MR = MC, which is less than the quantity where demand meets MC. For the units between, buyers value each unit (demand) more than it costs to make (MC), but they are not produced. The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and MC over those units.
earns.why: It names and bounds the region and explains the units lost.

misses.answer: The deadweight loss is the monopoly's profit, the area that buyers lose.
misses.why: Profit is a transfer to the monopoly, not a loss to everyone; the deadweight loss is the triangle past the monopoly quantity.

why.1: ATC bounds the profit rectangle, not the loss.
why.2: MR is not the value to buyers; demand is.

units.label: Over the units from
options: the monopoly quantity to where demand meets MC

why.1: Those units are produced; the loss is on units not produced.

prompts.title: Perfect price discrimination
prompts.prompt: Explain what happens to output, consumer surplus and deadweight loss when a monopolist can charge each buyer the most that buyer will pay.
checklist: Says output rises to where demand meets MC
Says consumer surplus becomes producer surplus (falls to zero)
Says deadweight loss disappears

earns.answer: With perfect price discrimination, each extra sale does not lower the price on earlier ones, so marginal revenue equals the demand curve. The monopolist sells to every buyer who will pay at least MC, so output rises to where demand meets MC, deadweight loss disappears, and all of the consumer surplus becomes the firm's profit.
earns.why: It covers all three outcomes and why MR equals demand.

misses.answer: Prices are higher for everyone, so output falls and buyers are worse off.
misses.why: Some buyers pay less than the single price, and output rises to the efficient quantity.

q.label: Output
options: rises to where demand meets MC

why.1: Selling to more buyers at their own prices raises output.
Each buyer pays the most he or she will pay, so no surplus is left to buyers.
Output reaches the efficient quantity, so no trades are lost.

prompts.title: Monopolistic competition in the long run
prompts.prompt: Explain what happens in the long run to a monopolistically competitive restaurant that is earning economic profit.
checklist: Says profit attracts entry of new restaurants with close substitutes
Says the firm's demand (and MR) shifts left and becomes more elastic
Says this goes on until demand is tangent to ATC: zero economic profit

earns.answer: Economic profit attracts new restaurants, so entry adds close substitutes. Each takes some customers, so this restaurant's demand curve and MR shift left and become more elastic. Entry continues until demand is tangent to ATC, which leaves zero economic profit, with price still above MC.
earns.why: It gives entry, the shift in this firm's demand and the tangency end point.

misses.answer: In the long run the restaurant earns zero profit, like a perfectly competitive firm at minimum ATC.
misses.why: Zero profit is right, but it skips entry and the demand shift, and the firm does not end at minimum ATC.

why.1: Profit attracts firms rather than driving them out.

demand.label: The firm's demand
options: shifts left and becomes more elastic

end.label: Entry stops when demand is
options: equal to minimum ATC and MC

prompts.title: Prove a dominant strategy
prompts.prompt: Explain whether Altura has a dominant strategy in a game where Altura's payoffs are 30 (Advertise) or 20 (Do not) if Bexley advertises, and 50 (Advertise) or 45 (Do not) if Bexley does not.
checklist: Makes the comparison for Bexley advertising: 30 against 20
Makes the comparison for Bexley not advertising: 50 against 45
Concludes that advertising is dominant because it wins both

earns.answer: If Bexley advertises, Altura earns 30 > 20 by advertising. If Bexley does not advertise, Altura earns 50 > 45 by advertising. Advertising is better whatever Bexley does, so it is Altura's dominant strategy.
earns.why: Both comparisons are made with the numbers, one for each of Bexley's choices.

Makes the comparison for Altura not advertising: 40 against 45
Concludes that Bexley's best choice changes, so it has no dominant strategy

prompts.title: Check a cell for Nash equilibrium

Checks Nessa's switch: 9 against 6
Concludes that neither gains by switching alone, so it is a Nash equilibrium

earns.answer: Given that Nessa's opens late, Marlo's earns 12 > 7 by staying early. Given that Marlo's opens early, Nessa's earns 9 > 6 by staying late. Neither can gain by switching on its own, so (Open early, Open late) is a Nash equilibrium.

prompts.title: A tax that changes a dominant strategy

Makes both comparisons again with the new payoffs
Concludes that not advertising is now dominant

earns.answer: The tax lowers Altura's advertising payoffs to 30 - 15 = 15 and 50 - 15 = 35. If Bexley advertises, 20 > 15, so not advertising is better; if Bexley does not, 45 > 35, so again not advertising is better. Not advertising is now Altura's dominant strategy.
earns.why: It changes the right payoffs and makes both comparisons again.

prompts.title: Derived demand, link by link
prompts.prompt: Explain how a rise in the demand for fishing boats affects the wage and employment of welders who build them, in a competitive labor market.
checklist: Product demand rises, so the price of boats (MR) rises
MRP = MP x P rises, so the demand for welders shifts right
The wage and employment of welders rise

earns.answer: Higher demand for boats raises the price of a boat, which raises the marginal revenue each boat brings. Since MRP = MP x P, each welder's MRP rises, so the demand for welders shifts right. With labor supply unchanged, the wage rises and more welders are employed.
earns.why: Every link is there: product demand, price, MRP, labor demand, then wage and employment.

misses.answer: More boats are wanted, so more welders are hired.
misses.why: It skips the price, MRP and the labor demand shift, and says nothing about the wage.

why.1: Each welder works as before; what rises first is the price of the boat.

mrp.label: So welders' MRP
options: rises, and labor demand shifts right

why.1: A higher product price raises MRP.
A rightward demand shift along upward supply raises both.

prompts.title: MRP from marginal product and price
prompts.prompt: Calculate the MRP of the next worker at a firm that sells in a competitive market at $4 a unit, if that worker adds 12 units, and say whether the firm should hire her at a wage of $40.
checklist: Uses MRP = MP x P (marginal revenue equals the price here)
Shows the numbers: 12 x $4
Compares MRP with the wage to decide

earns.answer: MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue, and in a competitive product market MR is the price: 12 x $4 = $48. That is above the $40 wage, so hiring her adds $8 to profit and the firm should hire her.
earns.why: It uses the right formula with the numbers and applies the hiring rule.

misses.answer: Her MRP is $4 x $40 = $160, so she is worth hiring.
misses.why: MRP multiplies marginal product by marginal revenue, not the price by the wage.

prompts.title: An increase in labor supply
prompts.prompt: Draw a correctly labeled graph of the market for nurses and show the effect of a rise in the number of trained nurses on the wage and employment.
checklist: Shifts labor supply to the right (SL1 to SL2)
Shows the wage falling and employment rising
Labels the axes Wage and Quantity of labor, and both supply curves

earns.answer: More trained nurses shifts the labor supply curve to the right, from SL1 to SL2. Labor demand does not change. At the new equilibrium the wage falls from W1 to W2 and the number of nurses employed rises from Q1 to Q2.
earns.why: It shifts the right curve the right way and reads both outcomes.

misses.answer: More nurses means hospitals want more nurses, so demand shifts right and the wage rises.
misses.why: More trained nurses adds to supply; hospitals' demand did not change.

why.1: Hospitals' MRP did not change; the number of workers did.
A rightward supply shift along downward demand lowers the wage.

prompts.title: A falling product price and labor demand
prompts.prompt: Explain how a fall in the price of strawberries affects the wage and employment of strawberry pickers, in a competitive labor market.
checklist: The lower product price lowers MR
MRP = MP x P falls, so the demand for pickers shifts left
The wage and employment of pickers fall

earns.answer: A lower price of strawberries lowers the marginal revenue of each basket picked. Because MRP = MP x P, each picker's MRP falls, which shifts the demand for pickers to the left. With supply unchanged, the wage falls and fewer pickers are employed.
earns.why: It links the product price to MRP, labor demand, then the wage and employment.

misses.answer: Strawberries are cheaper, so pickers are paid less.
misses.why: It leaves out the MRP and labor demand links, and the change in employment.

why.1: A lower price lowers MR, and MRP with it.
why.2: MRP is MP times the product price, so it changes.

why.1: Demand shifts left, so along upward supply both fall.

prompts.title: Cheaper machines that work with labor
prompts.prompt: Explain how a fall in the price of delivery vans, which drivers need to do their job, affects the demand for drivers.
checklist: Says firms buy more vans, a complement to drivers
Says each driver can deliver more, so MP and MRP rise
Says the demand for drivers shifts right, raising the wage and employment

earns.answer: Cheaper vans lead firms to use more of them, and vans and drivers are complements: each van needs a driver. So more drivers are needed and each one delivers more, which raises marginal product, and MRP = MP x P rises. The demand for drivers shifts right, so the wage and employment of drivers increase.
earns.why: It names the complement relationship and follows it to MRP and labor demand.

misses.answer: Cheaper vans replace drivers, so the demand for drivers falls.
misses.why: Vans and drivers work together here; a cheaper complement raises the demand for labor.

why.1: A driver is needed for each van, so they are used together.
With more vans and a higher MRP, firms want more drivers.

prompts.title: Hire where MRP = MRC
prompts.prompt: Explain how many workers a firm in a competitive labor market hires at a wage of $30 if the MRP of the 3rd, 4th and 5th workers is $45, $30 and $20.
checklist: States the rule: hire up to MRP = MRC
Says MRC equals the wage for a wage taker
Gives the number: 4 workers

earns.answer: A firm hires up to MRP = MRC, and a wage taker's MRC is the wage, $30. The 3rd worker adds $45 for $30 and the 4th $30 for $30, so both are hired; the 5th adds $20, less than $30, so she is not. The firm hires 4 workers.
earns.why: It states the rule, says MRC is the wage and checks each worker.

misses.answer: The firm hires 3 workers, since the 3rd has the highest MRP.
misses.why: The test is MRP against MRC for each added worker; the 4th still covers her wage.

why.1: The largest MRP is only the first worker; keep hiring while MRP covers MRC.
why.2: MP is output, not a cost to compare with.

why.1: The 4th worker's MRP equals the wage, so hiring her does not lower profit.
why.2: The 5th worker's MRP is below the wage.

prompts.title: The firm's labor supply in a competitive market
prompts.prompt: Draw side-by-side graphs of a competitive labor market and one firm in it, and explain the firm's labor supply curve.
checklist: Shows the market wage set where market labor demand meets labor supply
Draws the firm's labor supply as horizontal at that wage, S = MFC = W
Shows the firm hiring where MRP meets that line

earns.answer: On the market graph the wage is set where labor demand meets labor supply. The firm is a wage taker, so on its own graph labor supply is a horizontal line at that wage, labeled S = MFC = W: each added worker costs the same wage. The firm hires where its MRP curve meets the line.
earns.why: It ties the firm's line to the market wage, labels it and shows the hire.

misses.answer: The firm's labor supply slopes up like the market supply of labor.
misses.why: One firm in a competitive market can hire as many as it wants at the market wage, so its supply is horizontal.

That sets the wage, not the firm's hiring.

prompts.title: The least-cost mix of inputs
prompts.prompt: Explain whether a firm is using the least-cost mix of labor and capital if the last worker adds 30 units at a wage of $15 and the last machine adds 50 units at a rental price of $20.

Compares output per dollar for each input
Says to use more of the input with more output per dollar

earns.answer: Compare marginal product per dollar: labor gives 30 / $15 = 2 units per dollar and capital gives 50 / $20 = 2.5 units per dollar. The two are not equal, so the mix is not least-cost: the firm should use more capital and less labor until output per dollar is equal for both.

Capital gives 2.5 units per dollar against labor's 2.

prompts.title: A monopsony's hire and wage

Hires 4: the 5th worker's MFC is above her MRP
Reads the wage down on labor supply: $12, not the MRP or the MFC

earns.answer: A monopsonist hires up to MRP = MFC. The 4th worker adds $20 for $18, so she is hired; the 5th adds $16 for $22, so she is not. The firm hires 4 workers and pays the wage labor supply needs for 4: $12, below both MRP and MFC.

prompts.title: A minimum wage in a monopsony

Says the firm now hires where MRP meets the minimum wage
Concludes that employment rises

earns.answer: Up to the number of workers willing to work at the minimum wage, each worker costs the same wage, so MFC becomes flat at the minimum wage. The monopsonist now hires where MRP meets that wage, which is more workers than before. Employment rises, unlike with a minimum wage above equilibrium in a competitive market.
earns.why: It explains the flat MFC and why the hire increases.

prompts.title: A negative externality and its fix
prompts.prompt: Explain how the market quantity of electricity from a polluting plant compares with the efficient quantity, and what policy would correct it.
checklist: Says MSC is above the private supply (MPC) by the cost to others
Says the market produces more than the efficient quantity where MSB = MSC
Names a per-unit tax equal to the external cost per unit

earns.answer: Pollution is a cost to others, so the marginal social cost (MSC) is above the plant's private cost (MPC). The market produces where demand meets MPC, more than the efficient quantity where MSB = MSC, which creates a deadweight loss. A per-unit tax equal to the external cost per unit shifts private supply up to MSC and brings output down to the efficient quantity.
earns.why: It compares the two quantities, names the deadweight loss and the corrective tax.

options: a per-unit tax equal to the external cost

why.1: A tax lowers output further from the efficient quantity.

prompts.title: The size of a corrective tax
prompts.prompt: Calculate the per-unit tax that brings a factory's output to the efficient quantity if its pollution does $3 of harm to others for each unit, and explain the result.
checklist: Sets the tax equal to the external cost per unit: $3
Says the tax raises the firm's private cost to the social cost
Says the market then produces where MSB = MSC

earns.answer: The external cost is $3 a unit, so the corrective tax is $3 per unit. It raises the factory's private marginal cost by $3, up to the marginal social cost, so the market now produces where demand (MSB) meets MSC: the efficient quantity, with no deadweight loss.
earns.why: It sizes the tax from the external cost and explains what it does to output.

misses.answer: The tax should be large enough to stop the factory from polluting at all.
misses.why: The efficient quantity is not zero output; the tax equals the harm per unit, $3.

tax.label: The tax per unit
options: large enough to stop all output

why.1: Some output is worth its full social cost; the tax prices the harm, $3.

result.label: With the tax the market produces

why.1: The efficient quantity is where MSB meets MSC, not zero.

prompts.title: Why markets underprovide public goods
prompts.prompt: Explain why a private firm would provide too little of a flood wall that protects a whole town.
checklist: Says the wall is nonexcludable: people who do not pay are still protected
Says it is nonrival: one more person protected costs nothing extra
Names the free-rider problem: few would pay, so the firm cannot cover its costs

earns.answer: The flood wall is nonexcludable, since the firm cannot stop people who do not pay from being protected, and nonrival, since protecting one more household costs nothing extra. So people have a reason to free ride, few would pay, and a private firm could not cover its costs, so it would provide too little.
earns.why: It names both properties and the free-rider problem that follows.

misses.answer: A private firm would not build it because flood walls are too expensive.
misses.why: High cost is not the reason; the problem is that people who do not pay still benefit.

why.1: Everyone behind the wall is protected, paying or not.
Diminishing returns are about production, not about who pays.

prompts.title: Overuse of a common resource
prompts.prompt: Explain why a lake open to anyone who wants to fish is likely to be overfished.
checklist: Says the fish are rival: a fish caught by one person cannot be caught by another
Says the lake is nonexcludable: no one can be kept from fishing
Says each fisher ignores the cost to others, so the lake is overused

earns.answer: Fish in an open lake are rival, because each fish one person catches is a fish no one else can catch, and nonexcludable, because anyone may fish. Each fisher weighs only his own catch and ignores the cost of fewer fish for everyone else, so together they take more than is efficient and the lake is overfished.
earns.why: It names both properties and the cost each fisher ignores.

misses.answer: The lake is overfished because fish are a public good.
misses.why: A public good is nonrival; fish are rival, which makes the lake a common resource.

why.1: A fish caught by one person is gone for others.
Public goods are nonrival.
why.2: Club goods are excludable.

prompts.title: A lump-sum tax on a monopoly
prompts.prompt: Explain how a lump-sum tax on a monopoly changes its MC and ATC curves, its output and its price.
checklist: Says a lump-sum tax is a fixed cost: ATC shifts up
Says MC does not change with a lump-sum tax
Says output and price stay where MR = MC, and profit falls

earns.answer: A lump-sum tax is paid whatever the firm produces, so it is a fixed cost: ATC shifts up and MC does not move. Since MR and MC are unchanged, the monopoly keeps producing where MR = MC and charges the same price from demand. Only its profit falls, by the amount of the tax.
earns.why: It separates the curves that move and follows through to output, price and profit.

misses.answer: The tax raises costs, so the monopoly cuts output and raises its price.
misses.why: A lump-sum tax leaves MC in place, so output and price do not change.

why.1: A lump-sum tax does not change with output, so MC stays.
That is what a per-unit tax would do, by raising MC.

prompts.title: Regulating a monopoly to the efficient quantity
prompts.prompt: Explain what a price ceiling set where demand meets MC does to a monopoly's output and to deadweight loss.
checklist: Says the ceiling makes MR flat at that price up to demand
Says the monopoly now produces where demand meets MC
Says the deadweight loss is removed

earns.answer: With a ceiling at the price where demand meets MC, the monopoly cannot charge more, so its marginal revenue is flat at that price up to the demand curve. It produces where that price equals MC, the quantity where demand meets MC. That is the efficient quantity, so the deadweight loss is removed.
earns.why: It explains the new MR, the new output and the efficiency result.

misses.answer: The ceiling lowers the price, so the monopoly produces less and there is a shortage.
misses.why: At this ceiling the monopoly produces more, up to where demand meets MC, with no shortage.

q.label: Output
options: rises to where demand meets MC

why.1: With a flat MR at the ceiling, the firm produces more, not less.
Output reaches the efficient quantity.

prompts.title: Reading a Lorenz curve point
prompts.prompt: Calculate the point on the Lorenz curve at 40 percent of households, if the lowest fifth of households receive 5 percent of income and the second fifth 10 percent, and compare it with the line of equality.
checklist: Adds the shares from the bottom: 5% + 10%
Plots the point at 40% of households and 15% of income
Says the line of equality would be at 40%, so income is unequal

earns.answer: A Lorenz curve is cumulative, so at 40 percent of households income is 5% + 10% = 15%. The point is (40%, 15%). On the line of equality it would be 40%, so the curve lies below the line and income is unequally shared.
earns.why: It adds the shares from the bottom and compares with the line of equality.

misses.answer: At 40 percent of households, income is 10 percent, the second fifth's share.
misses.why: A Lorenz curve adds the shares from the bottom; the second fifth alone is not the point.

why.1: That is the second fifth alone.
why.2: That is the line of equality.

cmp.label: Against the line of equality, the curve is

why.1: 15% is less than 40%, so the curve lies below the line.

prompts.title: Taxes and transfers and the Lorenz curve
prompts.prompt: Explain how a more progressive income tax, with the revenue paid as transfers to low-income households, changes the Lorenz curve for income after taxes and transfers.
checklist: Says income moves from high-income to low-income households
Says the lower shares rise, so the curve moves toward the line of equality
Says the Gini coefficient falls

earns.answer: A more progressive tax takes a larger share of high incomes, and the transfers raise low incomes. The shares of the lower groups rise, so the after-tax Lorenz curve moves toward the line of equality, and the Gini coefficient, which measures the area between the line and the curve as a share, falls.
earns.why: It explains the shift in income shares and the direction the curve moves.

misses.answer: The tax lowers everyone's income, so the Lorenz curve moves away from the line of equality.
misses.why: The transfers raise low incomes, so the curve moves toward the line, not away.

dir.label: The Lorenz curve moves
options: away from the line of equality

why.1: Income is shared more equally after the transfers.
A curve closer to the line means a smaller Gini coefficient.

prompts.title: Label a graph so the reader can score it
prompts.prompt: Draw a correctly labeled graph showing how the quantity a store sells of a good changes as its price changes, and say what each axis shows.
checklist: Puts price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis
Labels the curve and marks any point the question names on both axes
Uses the names in the question, not a letter alone, for each axis

earns.answer: On my graph the vertical axis is labeled "Price" and the horizontal axis "Quantity". The curve slopes down and is labeled D. The point at the current price is marked P1 on the price axis and Q1 on the quantity axis, so a reader can see both values.
earns.why: Both axes are named, the curve is labeled and the point is marked on each axis, which is what a reader checks first.

misses.answer: I drew a line going down from left to right, with x and y on the axes.
misses.why: x and y are not economic labels, the curve has no name and no point is marked, so the graph earns nothing.

why.1: Quantity goes on the horizontal axis.
why.2: A bare y is not a label a reader can score.

point.label: A point the question names is marked
options: on both axes, as P1 and Q1

why.1: Without P1 and Q1 on the axes, the values cannot be read or compared.

prompts.title: The slope of a line from two points
prompts.prompt: Calculate the slope of a straight line that passes through the points (2, 30) and (6, 50), and show your work.
checklist: Divides the change in the vertical value by the change in the horizontal value
Uses the same order for both changes (second point minus first)
States the slope with its sign: positive here

earns.answer: Slope is the rise over the run: (50 - 30) / (6 - 2) = 5. Both changes take the second point minus the first, and the slope is positive, so the line rises by 5 for each 1 it moves to the right.
earns.why: It shows the formula with the numbers and gives the sign, so the work earns the point.

misses.answer: The slope is 20 because the line goes from 30 up to 50.
misses.why: That is the rise alone; the run of 4 is not divided out, so the number is wrong and no work is shown.

top.label: On top of the fraction
options: the change in the vertical value, 50 - 30
the change in the horizontal value, 6 - 2

why.1: That is the run; slope is rise over run.
Both values rise together, so the slope is positive.
why.2: 20 is the rise alone; divide by the run of 4.

prompts.title: A shift of the curve or a move along it
prompts.prompt: Explain how a change in a good's own price and a change in something else that buyers care about appear differently on a graph of price and quantity.
checklist: Says a change in the good's own price is a movement along the curve
Says a change in anything else buyers care about shifts the whole curve
Names the new curve or the new point (D2, or a point further along D1)

earns.answer: A change in the good's own price is a movement along the curve, because price is on an axis: the point slides along D1. A change in something else buyers care about, such as their incomes, shifts the whole curve, and I label the new curve D2.
earns.why: It separates the two cases and says why: the price is on an axis, other causes are not.

misses.answer: When the price changes the curve moves, and when other things change the curve moves too.
misses.why: It does not say which change is a movement along the curve and which is a shift, so neither case is right.

price.label: A change in the good's own price is

why.1: Price is on an axis, so its change moves along the curve.

other.label: A change in buyers' incomes is
options: a shift of the whole curve

why.1: Income is not on an axis, so the whole curve moves to a new position.

prompts.title: Shade and size a triangle between two lines
prompts.prompt: Calculate the area of the triangle between two lines that cross, where its base runs 4 units along the horizontal axis and its height is 6 units, and say what the shading must cover.
checklist: Uses one half times base times height for a triangle
Shows the numbers: 1/2 x 4 x 6
Says the shading covers the whole triangle between the lines

earns.answer: A triangle's area is 1/2 x base x height, so 1/2 x 4 x 6 = 12 square units. On the graph I shade the whole triangle between the two lines, from where they cross out to the base, not part of it.
earns.why: The one half is there, the numbers are shown, and the shading covers the whole region.

misses.answer: The area is 4 x 6 = 24, and I shaded the space near where the lines cross.
misses.why: It leaves out the one half that a triangle needs, and partial shading loses the point.

formula.label: The area of a triangle is

why.1: That is a rectangle; a triangle is half of it.

shade.label: Shade
options: the whole triangle between the lines

why.1: Readers score the whole region; part of it loses the point.
